title: Climbing the compression ladder
intro: Thirty filings, one question, three rungs of compression. Each rung is cheaper than the last — and one of them is not a saving at all, because the fidelity assertion catches it dropping the identifier the answer depends on.

provenance.source: a narrated compression ladder over one debtor's filing history; token counts and prices are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: The pipeline this walks is M18's A Three-Stage Compression Pipeline — prune, then extract verbatim, then abstract only the remainder, with an assertion on every identifier.

steps.title: The source — thirty filings, one question
narrative: The question is narrow: which liens are still active against ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C., and who holds them? The material is not narrow — thirty filings going back to 2011, at 41,800 tokens.

Sent whole, it works. It costs about fourteen cents a call, it is slow, and the five facts that matter are spread thinly through the most crowded part of the window. This is your baseline and your correctness reference: whatever compression you do next has to match this answer.
steps.youDo: Before compressing anything, write down the exact facts the answer must contain. That list is what you will assert on later.

steps.title: Rung 1 — prune
narrative: Twenty-five of the thirty filings carry status: terminated. The question asked about active liens. Drop them.

Pruning is the safest rung because it rephrases nothing — it only removes units that were never relevant. That is also its ceiling: you can compress exactly as far as your irrelevant material goes and not one token further. Here that is 69%, for free.
steps.claudeSays: I did not summarize anything. I filtered on a field. Every token that survived is byte-identical to the source.
steps.youDo: Run the cheapest filter you have — status, date range, document type — before you reach for a summarizer. Most contexts are 40-70% irrelevant.

terminal.text: active = [f for f in filings if f["status"] == "active"]
5 active liens returned, all five secured parties correct

steps.title: Rung 2 — extract verbatim
narrative: Each surviving filing is still a full document: addresses, collateral clauses, boilerplate about proceeds. The question needs three spans per filing — the filing ID, the secured party, and the filing date.

Extraction keeps those spans exactly as written and deletes the rest. 12,900 tokens become 3,400. Nothing was reworded, so 2024-FL-0012345 is still 2024-FL-0012345 and FIRST CAPITAL EQUIPMENT FINANCE, INC. still has its comma and its INC.
steps.claudeSays: Extraction shortens only by deletion. That bounds how small it can get — and it is also the reason it cannot corrupt an identifier.

steps.title: Rung 3 — abstract, and the receipt that looks best
narrative: One more rung. Hand the whole history to a summarizer and ask for a compact restatement. It comes back at 640 tokens — a 98.5% reduction against the baseline, under two cents a call, and it reads beautifully.
If you stop here you will ship it. The receipt is the best one on the page: cheapest input, lowest latency, fluent output. Nothing on this screen tells you anything is wrong.

steps.title: The fidelity assertion fires
narrative: Run the check the pipeline was built with: every active filing ID must appear, character for character, in the compressed block. Two are missing. 2024-FL-0019988 was generalized to "a freight-capital lender", and two distinct liens were merged into one clause.

So the answer built on that rollup names three secured parties instead of five, and cannot cite a single filing number. The output is 88% cheaper and wrong. A saving that loses a required fact is not a saving.

This is measurable, not just arguable. The successor course grades exactly this: its compressed arm answered an aggregation question in 208 input tokens against a naive arm's 1,700 — but it dropped the required facts PA-1004 and MANUAL_REVIEW, and the grader marked it FAIL with the savings void. The naive arm passed.
steps.claudeSays: The assertion is three lines and it runs before the call, not after. It is the difference between a compression pipeline and a hope.
steps.youDo: Add assert f["filing_id"] in block for every load-bearing record in your own compressor, and let it raise.

terminal.text:
for f in active:
    assert f["filing_id"] in block, f"LOST identifier {f['filing_id']}!"

steps.title: Where the ladder actually stops
narrative: The shipped pipeline is not the cheapest rung — it is the cheapest rung that passes. Prune the terminated filings, extract the five active records verbatim, and abstract only the routine history into one line: "25 routine filings (2011-2018), all terminated".

That block is 3,900 tokens — 8,260 input tokens once the rules and tools are counted, at $0.0280 a call. That is 80% below the baseline, with every identifier byte-identical and the assertion green. The abstraction is still there; it is just pointed at the material that can tolerate it.

The rule to carry out of this module: match the technique to the content's fidelity requirement. Prune what is irrelevant, extract what a decision turns on, abstract the tolerant remainder — and never ship a compression ratio you have not graded.
steps.youDo: Split your own context into three buckets — droppable, must-be-verbatim, tolerant-of-rewriting — and apply exactly one technique to each.

view.text: Cheapest is not the goal; cheapest-that-passes is. Prune what is irrelevant, extract what the decision turns on, abstract only the routine remainder — and put an assertion between the compressor and the model, because a summary that lost an identifier fails silently and reads perfectly.
